stages.name: Regulation
stages.title: Regulation
stages.sub: Weigh up the strengths and weaknesses of using rules to fix market failure.

steps.q: A government bans waste discharge above a fixed amount and fines those who break it. What kind of intervention is this?
steps.right: A legal rule the government sets and enforces
steps.wrong: A tax that makes the waste more expensive to produce
steps.hint: The government is not charging money here, it is banning behaviour outright.

steps.q: The law caps waste at 10 tonnes a month, checked by inspectors. Compared with asking nicely, is the rule exact?
steps.right: Yes, the limit is exact and checkable
steps.wrong: No, it is still open to interpretation
steps.hint: Think about whether 'no more than 10 tonnes' leaves room for doubt.

steps.q: Compared with building a whole new tax system to price pollution, how quickly can a ban like this be written and passed?
steps.right: It can be done fairly fast
steps.wrong: It takes just as long either way
steps.hint: Passing one law versus designing a tax rate, collection system and enforcement mechanism from scratch.

steps.right: No, it costs money and staff to check
steps.wrong: Yes, once the law exists it runs itself
steps.hint: A rule on paper only works if someone checks whether it is being followed.

steps.q: Facing a strict waste ban, some factories secretly pay an unlicensed firm to dump waste at night. What does the ban lead to?
steps.right: An illegal market springs up to dodge the rule
steps.wrong: The factories simply cut their output as intended
steps.hint: The rule did not remove the desire to dump waste cheaply, it just made the legal route costly.

steps.q: Over time the regulator hires ex-factory managers and the waste limit quietly relaxes to suit the industry. What has happened to it?
steps.right: The regulator has been influenced by the industry it regulates
steps.wrong: The regulator has simply become more efficient
steps.hint: Who ends up shaping the rules, the public interest or the firms being regulated?
